title: Facet-selective ballistic supercurrent in a weak topological insulator
authors: Prasanna Rout, Ankit Khola, Lalit Pandey, Paolo Sessi, Xiaochun Huang, Ivo Cools, S. Galeski, Matthias Bode, Johan Åkerman, Floriana Lombardi, Thilo Bauch, Saroj P. Dash
abstract: Topological superconductivity is widely pursued by inducing superconducting correlations in topologically protected boundary states. In two dimensions, this strategy has been realized using one-dimensional topological edge modes, but in three-dimensional crystals, spatially separated surface supercurrents confined to selected facets have not yet been achieved. Here we demonstrate facet-selective ballistic supercurrent in Josephson junctions based on the weak topological insulator ZrTe<sub>5</sub>. Superconducting quantum interferometry reveals SQUID-like critical current oscillations with flux-quantum periodicity, establishing that the supercurrent is spatially concentrated on specific crystallographic facets that host gapless topological surface states. Rotating the magnetic field yields markedly distinct interference patterns, linking the supercurrent distribution to the underlying bulk topology. The exponential temperature dependence of the critical current and triangular interference lobes provide signatures of ballistic transport due to high-transmission topological channels. These results establish weak topological insulators as a platform for facet-resolved superconducting devices and higher-order topological superconductivity.
summary: The research demonstrates the existence of supercurrents confined specifically to certain facets of a weak topological insulator ($	ext{ZrTe}_5$). By using superconducting interferometry, the authors confirmed that this facet-selectivity and ballistic nature are direct consequences of the material's underlying bulk topology. This establishes WTIs as a promising platform for designing next-generation, topologically controlled superconducting devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is to demonstrate and characterize facet-selective ballistic supercurrent flow in three-dimensional weak topological insulators (WTIs). This addresses the challenge of confining superconducting currents to specific crystal facets.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated SQUID-like critical current oscillations confined to specific crystallographic facets, confirming that the supercurrent is dictated by the underlying bulk topology of the WTI material ($	ext{ZrTe}_5$).
method: Superconducting quantum interferometry was performed on Josephson junctions formed with $	ext{ZrTe}_5$, supplemented by STM/STS measurements and analysis of magnetic field dependence.
model_or_system: The system utilizes Weak Topological Insulators ($	ext{ZrTe}_5$), which possess gapless topological surface states only on selected facets, contrasting with Strong TIs. Superconductivity is induced via proximity coupling in Josephson junctions.
key_observables: SQUID-like critical current oscillations ($I_c$ vs $B$), exponential temperature dependence of $I_c$, and distinct interference patterns dependent on the magnetic field orientation relative to crystal facets.
important_parameters: The supercurrent is confined to specific side facets, exhibiting ballistic transport signatures characterized by an exponential temperature dependence ($\exp(-\pi^2 k_B T / \delta E)$).
main_assumptions: The measurements assume that the observed superconducting current flow is dominated by the topological surface states rather than trivial bulk conduction channels.
figures_summary: Figures show SQUID-like $I$-$V$ curves and interference patterns (Fig. 4) confirming facet confinement, alongside STM/STS data showing a bulk gap and enhanced LDOS at step edges (Fig. 2).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical basis for WTI surface currents, details the experimental setup using Josephson junctions on $	ext{ZrTe}_5$, presents measurements confirming SQUID oscillations and field-orientation dependence, and concludes by establishing WTIs as a platform for facet-resolved superconducting devices.
why_interesting: This work provides direct experimental evidence linking bulk topological invariants (WTI classification) to macroscopic quantum phenomena (supercurrent distribution), which is highly relevant for understanding engineered quantum materials interfaces.
